title: Serenus asks for help
hook: On Tranquility opens with a friend confessing he is neither sick nor well (On Tranquility 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was vale, and sixty letters folded, Lucilius' half left blank. Your line was write back.

Nothing's wrong, exactly. No crisis. Nobody would call a helpline. But not okay either. Some days a simple life looks right; other days a scroll through other people's kitchens leaves a person feeling a little poorer. Things get started and dropped. A restlessness with no name. A friend of Seneca's named Serenus wrote him a letter describing exactly that, and Seneca made it the opening of a whole book, On Tranquility of Mind. Our first essay starts with somebody else's honesty.
screen: `NOTHING'S WRONG, EXACTLY.` → `NOT OKAY EITHER.` → `A FRIEND WRITES IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, the confession. When Serenus looks at himself honestly, he says, some faults are out in the open, some are hidden, and some come and go. He isn't free of the things he dislikes in himself, and he isn't fully their slave either. He's neither sick nor well. Second, the details. He loves plain living: a simple servant, plain dishes, nothing for show. Then he visits a rich house, all polished floors and crowds of servants, and comes home not worse, he says, but sadder. He resolves to go into public life; one setback and he wants to retreat. He decides to write plainly; then grand phrases carry him off. Third, his image. It isn't a storm that troubles me, Serenus says, it's seasickness: the sea is calm, and still the stomach turns. And then the plainest line of all: if you have any remedy, please. Fourth, Seneca's name for the cure. What Serenus wants, he answers, is something the Greek thinker Democritus called euthymia, good spirits, a steady mind. Seneca gives it a Latin name: tranquillitas, calm. Not excitement, not numbness. A mind on level ground, at peace with itself. Notice how the book begins. Not with a lecture. With a friend willing to describe, plainly, a trouble he couldn't name.
screen: `NOT FREE, NOT FULLY A SLAVE.` · `PLAIN LIVING, THEN A RICH HOUSE.` · `NOT A STORM: SEASICKNESS.` · `EUTHYMIA, TRANQUILLITAS, CALM.` · then, large: `NEITHER SICK NOR WELL.`

segments.voice: Describe your own unsettledness to yourself as precisely as Serenus did, not why, just what it's like: where it shows up, what you want one day and drop the next, whether it's a storm or calm-sea seasickness. Find one honest sentence, the kind you'd only write to a good friend; naming it is the first page.
Serenus. The friend whose honest letter, confessing he's neither sick nor well, opens Seneca's book On Tranquility of Mind. Today's word.
Your line: neither sick nor well. The whole book began with someone asking. That's day four hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Readers of On Tranquility of Mind sometimes begin, as Serenus did, by describing their own restlessness honestly before looking for any remedy.

chat.says: Nothing's wrong, but I feel restless and drifty. Did any old writer get that?
options: Serenus did; he called it seasickness on a calm sea, and asked Seneca for help.
Seneca said that kind of restlessness only troubles people who are lazy.
Serenus said it came from storms in his life that he'd never faced.
chat.meaning: Serenus says he's neither sick nor well: not a storm, but seasickness on a calm sea. His honest plea opens On Tranquility of Mind.

tranquillitas.meaning: Latin: calm, a mind at peace with itself

notes: On Tranquility 1 paraphrased: Serenus' faults (open, hidden, intermittent), neither sick nor well, love of plain living vs a rich house (returns 'not worse but sadder'), public life and retreat, plain vs grand style, 'not tempest but seasickness' (1.17), and the plea for a remedy. Confirm.
On Tranquility 2.3: Democritus' euthymia, rendered tranquillitas. Confirm.
Serenus' identity (Annaeus Serenus, Seneca's friend, prefect of the night watch, died young; see Letter 63) is not stated in the script.
Plutarch's 'On Tranquility of Mind' (Peri Euthymias) mentioned in the trapdoor. Confirm.
American spelling 'On Tranquility' used throughout; the outline uses 'Tranquillity'.
